title: Hypothermia and frostbite
summary: Signs of hypothermia and frostbite, how to warm someone safely, and what not to do.

sources.title: CDC - Avoid, Spot, Treat Frostbite and Hypothermia
CDC Yellow Book - Heat and Cold Illness in Travelers (first aid)

blocks.text: **Hypothermia is an emergency.** If someone's temperature is below **95°F**, or they are confused, slurring words or very drowsy, get medical attention right away. Treat hypothermia first if frostbite is also present.

Hypothermia is most likely in very cold weather, but it can happen above 40°F if a person is wet from rain, sweat or cold water and gets chilled. Older adults without enough food, clothing or heat, and babies sleeping in cold rooms, are at higher risk.

items: Adults: shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech, drowsiness
Infants: bright red, cold skin and very low energy
Worsening hypothermia brings more confusion, clumsiness and eventually coma
Get the person into a warm room or shelter.
Warm them under dry layers of blankets and clothing. Warm the chest, neck, head and groin first. Skin-to-skin contact under dry layers also works.
Get medical attention as soon as you can. CDC's clinician guide adds that someone with mild hypothermia should not stand or walk for 30 minutes.
Redness or pain in any skin area can be the first sign
A white or grayish-yellow patch of skin
Skin that feels unusually firm or waxy
Numbness. The person often does not know, because frozen tissue is numb
Get into a warm place and remove wet clothing.
Put the frostbitten areas in warm-to-touch water. For a thermometer, CDC's clinician guide gives 98.6 to 102.2°F (37 to 39°C). Without one, test the water on uninjured skin so it is not scalding.
Dress the area loosely and see a health care provider. Rewarming can be very painful, so pain relief may help.
Do not let it thaw and refreeze. If refreezing is possible, wait to rewarm.

blocks.text: Frostbitten skin is numb and burns easily. Do not rub or massage it. Do not use a heating pad, electric blanket, fireplace, heat lamp, radiator or stove for warming. Do not walk on frostbitten feet or toes unless you must.
Never use insulin that has frozen. See the insulin storage guide for how to keep it from freezing in a cold home.
